planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in cool, acidic, humus-rich soil with sharp drainage; this true alpine resents hot, humid summers and performs best in mountain or northern gardens.

directions: This dense, low-growing evergreen from the European Alps takes its name from the rust-colored scaly coating on the underside of its glossy dark leaves. Small rose-pink to crimson bell flowers cluster at the branch tips in early to mid summer, appearing just above the tidy foliage mound. Unlike many rhododendrons it forms sprawling subalpine colonies and genuinely struggles where summers are hot and humid, so give it a cool site with excellent drainage. Keep soil acidic and evenly moist without ever letting the shallow crown sit wet through winter.

planting.note: Plant in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil; this low, spreading species is among the hardiest rhododendron species and has long been valued for breeding cold-tolerant garden hybrids.

directions: Native to the high mountains of the Caucasus and northeastern Turkey, this low, broad-spreading evergreen carries leathery leaves with a thin, pale woolly coating on their undersides that helps it withstand harsh winters. Creamy white to soft yellow or blush bell-shaped flowers open in dense trusses in mid-spring. Its exceptional cold hardiness has made it a historically important parent for hardy garden hybrids bred to survive far colder winters than most showy rhododendrons tolerate. Grow it in acidic, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture and light shade, especially where summers run hot.

planting.note: Plant in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; this exceptionally cold-hardy species tolerates harsher winters than most broadleaf evergreen shrubs and is valued as breeding stock for cold climates.

directions: Found growing wild on the high mountains of Japan, this large, rounded evergreen shrub carries thick, leathery leaves with a thin brown indumentum beneath and is prized for tolerating colder winters than nearly any other broadleaf rhododendron species. Loose trusses of funnel-shaped flowers, ranging from white through soft pink, open later in early summer than most rhododendrons, extending the woodland bloom season. Because of its extreme hardiness it has been widely used by breeders developing cold-climate hybrids able to survive far north of where typical species rhododendrons thrive. Plant in acidic, moisture-retentive soil in dappled shade and avoid waterlogged sites.

planting.note: Plant in deep, acidic, humus-rich soil with room to mature into a large multi-stemmed shrub; among the more adaptable and floriferous of the big Chinese species.

directions: Native to the mountain forests of Sichuan and Yunnan, this large, smooth-leaved evergreen shrub produces generously sized trusses of fragrant white to soft pink funnel-shaped flowers in late spring, with a true scent that many showier hybrids lack. It matures into a substantial, rounded specimen and flowers more reliably at a younger age than many other big-leaf Chinese species. Give it deep, acidic, well-drained soil with consistent moisture and dappled shade, siting it where its eventual bulk will not crowd smaller woodland neighbors. Its relative garden tolerance and fragrance have made it a favored parent species for hardier, scented hybrids.

planting.note: Plant in sheltered woodland soil with deep, acidic, humus-rich conditions and protection from late spring frost, since this species flowers very early and the show can be lost to a hard freeze.

directions: One of the most architectural of the big-leaf Chinese species, this slow-growing evergreen eventually takes on a tree-like form with whorls of long, glossy leaves radiating from the branch tips. Very early in spring, often before most other rhododendrons stir, large domed trusses of white to pale pink flowers with a deeper crimson blotch open on bare winter wood. Because flowering happens so early, a late hard frost can damage or destroy the display, so a sheltered site away from cold pockets is important. Give it deep, acidic, well-drained woodland soil and patience, since it takes years to reach its full stature.

planting.note: Plant in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in a sheltered woodland site; a compact, cool-climate species that resents hot, dry summers.

directions: Native to the mountains along the Yunnan-Myanmar border, this compact evergreen shrub takes its name from waxy, bell-shaped flowers that recall oleander blooms, though colored a vivid blood-red to scarlet rather than pink or white. Rounded, blue-green leaves with a glaucous underside set off the flower clusters, which open in mid-spring against a backdrop of smaller, tidier foliage than most of its Chinese relatives. It has long been valued by breeders as a source of pure, saturated red flower color. Grow it in cool, acidic, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture and dappled shade, and protect it from scorching summer heat.

planting.note: Plant in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered spot; comparatively hardy and tidy-habited for a Chinese woodland species.

directions: This Sichuan native is instantly recognizable by its nearly perfectly round, heart-based blue-green leaves, a trait that gives the species its name and sets it apart from almost every other rhododendron. In mid-spring it produces nodding, bell-shaped flowers in a soft clear pink held in loose, open trusses against the rounded foliage. It grows into a broad, well-mannered mound rather than a lanky shrub, making it easier to place in smaller woodland gardens than many large-leaved relatives. Plant in acidic, moisture-retentive soil with dappled shade and shelter from drying wind.

planting.note: Plant in a sheltered site with acidic, well-drained soil; flowers open very early and can be damaged by hard spring frost, so avoid low-lying cold pockets.

directions: Named for the Moupin region of Sichuan where it was first collected, this compact evergreen shrub has small, glossy leaves and attractive peeling, cinnamon-colored bark on older stems. Very early in spring, often among the first rhododendrons to bloom, it opens fragrant white to pale pink flowers frequently marked with crimson spotting in the throat. Its small stature and tidy habit make it well suited to a sheltered spot near a path where its early scent can be appreciated up close. Choose a protected microclimate, since the precocious flowers are vulnerable to late frost damage.

planting.note: Plant in a raised bed or rock garden pocket with sharply drained, acidic, humus-rich soil; this creeping species resents heavy, wet ground.

directions: Collected high in the mountains along the Yunnan-Tibet border by plant hunter George Forrest, this creeping evergreen hugs the ground with rounded leaves that often take on a purplish cast in winter. Despite its tiny stature, it produces disproportionately large, waxy, deep scarlet bell flowers in spring, making it a dramatic accent for a rock garden or raised bed. Its trailing, mat-forming habit suits it to tumbling over rock edges or filling a shaded scree pocket rather than open border planting. Grow in gritty, acidic, well-drained soil and avoid letting the shallow roots dry out completely.

planting.note: Plant in a raised bed or rock garden with sharply drained, acidic, gritty soil; a dwarf alpine species that suffers in heavy, poorly drained ground.

directions: Native to high alpine slopes along the Myanmar-Tibet-Yunnan border, this dwarf, mat-forming evergreen has small, gray-green, scaly leaves and an unusually flat, open flower shape compared to most bell-flowered rhododendrons. In late spring it bears saucer-shaped blooms in rich purple-pink to magenta, held just above the low mound of foliage. Its naturally compact, mounding habit makes it a favorite for rock gardens, raised beds, and trough plantings rather than general shrub borders. Provide gritty, sharply drained, acidic soil and avoid summer waterlogging.
